phrases.translation: Successful indeed are the believers
phrases.explanation: The surah opens by announcing that the believers have truly prospered, and the emphatic construction treats this as settled news rather than a possibility. Prosperity here is not wealth or rank but reaching what Allah has promised. The verses that follow name the qualities of these believers, so the opening sentence also serves as a heading for the whole passage. Early reports even describe the Garden itself proclaiming these words when it was created.

phrases.translation: those who humble themselves in prayer
phrases.explanation: Humility in prayer is the first quality named, and the word used for it carries the sense of submission and lowering oneself before Allah. Reports tie the verse to companions who used to lift their eyes to the sky while praying and then lowered them once it was revealed. Early authorities disagreed about whether the humility meant stillness of the limbs, fear, or an inner state of the heart, and the commentary treats all of these as fitting the same attitude of submission.

phrases.translation: those who avoid idle talk
phrases.explanation: Idle talk translates a word covering anything vain or frivolous, and the verse describes not merely abstaining from it but turning away from it. Early explanations name falsehood, sins, and speech that invites blame. The point is an active refusal rather than passive innocence. Believers are pictured as people whose attention is not captured by what carries no benefit, so their hearing and their speech are kept for what is worthwhile.

phrases.translation: those who pay alms-tax
phrases.explanation: The alms-tax is the obligatory share of one's wealth that Allah has prescribed for the poor, and the wording stresses actually paying it rather than merely approving of it. Possessions are treated as something held in trust, so giving is not a favour but a duty attached to what one owns. Placing it among prayer, chastity, and honesty shows that worship in this surah includes how money is handled.

phrases.translation: those who guard their chastity
phrases.explanation: Guarding chastity is described with the image of protecting something valuable from being taken or exposed. The phrasing concerns the private parts specifically, so the quality is about bodily conduct rather than only inner intention. The commentary notes that the guarding is measured against what Allah has permitted and what He has forbidden, which the next verses spell out. It presents self-restraint as a discipline the believer keeps watch over.

phrases.translation: except with their wives
phrases.explanation: The exception opens the lawful side of the boundary just described. A wife is the first category named, so marriage is presented as the ordinary setting in which intimacy belongs. The verse does not treat desire itself as the problem, but its direction outside the permitted bond. Naming the spouse also assumes the rights and duties that marriage creates, since a wife is not simply a means of lawful pleasure but a partner with claims the surah goes on to protect.

phrases.translation: or those ˹bondwomen˺ in their possession,
phrases.explanation: Here the verse names a second category recognised in the society it addressed, women held in slavery, whose legal position was part of the world into which the Qur'an spoke. The text treats them as belonging to the household of the man who possessed them rather than as free partners in a contract. That institution has since disappeared, so the phrase describes a historical arrangement and its regulation, not a pattern for today.

phrases.translation: for then they are free from blame
phrases.explanation: The closing words remove any censure from a man who confines intimacy to these two categories. The commentary explains that blame applies only when someone goes past what is permitted to what is forbidden, so the verse is not praising appetite but defining its lawful limits. This prepares for the next verse, which condemns those who seek beyond the boundary as transgressors who step over the limit Allah set.

phrases.translation: but whoever seeks beyond that
phrases.explanation: The verse turns the boundary into a test of desire. Seeking beyond what has just been permitted is described as reaching for something deliberately out of bounds, and the Arabic image is of a person stretching past a limit. The commentary applies this to any sexual relation outside marriage and notes that the Qur'an calls such a person a transgressor. The standard is not private preference but the line Allah has drawn.

phrases.translation: are the transgressors
phrases.explanation: Transgressors translates a word for those who overstep, and the commentary is explicit that the overstepping is from what Allah allowed to what He forbade. The verse therefore does not leave the earlier permission open to extension by custom or convenience. It also shows how the surah pairs mercy with limits: the lawful is wide enough to live in, and the blame falls on the person who refuses to stay inside it.

phrases.translation: ˹the believers are also˺ those who are true
phrases.explanation: Trusts are the things other people place in one's care, whether property, secrets, or duties, and the wording takes in obligations that no contract records. Believers are described as the sort of people who can be relied on with what has been handed to them. The commentary explains the quality as safeguarding what was entrusted and fulfilling it. It also notes a difference among reciters over whether the word is read as one trust or many, and prefers the plural.

phrases.translation: to their trusts and covenants
phrases.explanation: Covenants are the agreements people make with one another, and the verse places them beside trusts so that both the unspoken and the spoken commitments of a believer are covered. The commentary describes this attentiveness as keeping every part of an agreement rather than only the part that is convenient. Set among the qualities that lead to Paradise, honesty in dealings becomes a religious duty rather than a matter of social reputation.

phrases.translation: and those who are ˹properly˺ observant of their prayers
phrases.explanation: The final quality returns to prayer, described here as something watched over and maintained. The commentary explains this as attending to the appointed times and not letting other occupations push the prayer aside until its moment has passed. Another explanation speaks of performing the prayers continually. Coming after the earlier mention of humility, it shows that prayer in this surah is both an inner attitude and a discipline kept up through the day.

phrases.translation: These are the ones who will be awarded
phrases.explanation: The Arabic word behind this promise is inheritance, and the commentary explains that such people receive the dwellings prepared for them in Paradise. A report attributed to the Prophet describes every person as having two homes, one in the Garden and one in the Fire, so that whoever is saved inherits what another would have had. The image turns the reward into something already set aside and waiting, claimed by those who lived as these verses describe.

phrases.translation: Paradise as their own.
phrases.explanation: The inheritance is identified as the Firdaws, the highest and most central part of Paradise, and the commentary notes that the word was used among the Arabs for a garden of grapevines. It also recalls a report about a grieving mother who was told that her son had reached the highest Firdaws. The reward is therefore a place prepared and named, not a vague promise of comfort.

phrases.translation: They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: The final note is permanence. The commentary reads the phrase as abiding in the garden without ever leaving it, which answers the fear that even the greatest reward might end. Together with the opening word about success, the passage closes a circle: the believers described in these verses are the ones whose prosperity is settled and unbroken, not a temporary advantage that passes with this life.

phrases.translation: And indeed, We created humankind
phrases.explanation: The account of human origins begins with clay. The commentary explains the extract as what is drawn out from every kind of earth, and notes that Adam was created from earth taken from its surface. The point of the image is that the human being, with all his faculties, begins from the simplest material. What follows traces the same descent through stages that everyone has passed through.

phrases.translation: from an extract of clay
phrases.explanation: The commentary records disagreement over who is meant by humankind here, with some holding that it is Adam and others that it is his descendants, created from an extract of Adam, that is, the semen drawn from his loins. The second view is preferred because the next verse places the same being in the womb. The verse therefore joins the first human to everyone who came after him.

phrases.translation: then placed each ˹human˺ as a sperm-drop
phrases.explanation: The next stage is placement. The human is made a sperm-drop in a secure resting place, which the commentary identifies as the womb where the fluid comes to rest. Describing the place as secure recalls the care built into the process, since the resting place was prepared beforehand for what would be placed in it. The smallness of the drop is set against the reliability of its setting.

phrases.translation: in a secure place
phrases.explanation: The place is secure because it has been arranged for what will develop there, and the commentary explains that it holds the drop until its appointed development is complete. The wording turns attention from the tiny beginning to the dependability of the whole arrangement. Nothing in the process is left to chance, and the next verse continues the sequence through the stages that follow.

phrases.translation: then We developed the drop into a clinging clot ˹of blood˺,
phrases.explanation: The stages are set out in order, each one turning the previous substance into something new. The commentary explains the clinging clot as congealed blood. The repetition of the same verb for shaping gives the passage a steady rhythm, as though the reader were watching a single process unfold rather than a series of unrelated events. Each step prepares the next one.

phrases.translation: then developed the clot into a lump ˹of flesh˺,
phrases.explanation: A lump of flesh follows the clot, and the commentary explains it as a small piece of flesh formed from what came before. Every stage is described as created from the one that preceded it, so nothing appears suddenly out of nowhere. The sequence is meant to be read as a single act of making, done in steps that anyone can recognise in the bodies around them.

phrases.translation: then developed the lump into bones, then clothed the bones with flesh,
phrases.explanation: Bones come next, and then flesh clothing them. The commentary notes a difference among reciters over whether the word for bones is read in the plural or the singular, and it prefers the plural because the majority read it so. The image is of a frame being assembled and then covered, the language of a craftsman rather than of accident, and the reader is expected to follow the work step by step.

phrases.translation: then We brought it into being as a new creation.
phrases.explanation: Then comes the decisive change. The formed body is brought into being as a new creation, and the commentary records two explanations, that this is the breathing of the soul into him or that it is the guiding of the person through the stages after birth, from infancy to maturity. It prefers the first, since by the soul he becomes a human being rather than a shape.

phrases.translation: So Blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators
phrases.explanation: The verse ends in praise. Blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators, and the commentary records disagreement over the sense of creators here, with one view that it means the best of makers, since the Arabs called every maker a creator. Another view connects it to the claim that Jesus created, and answers that Allah creates more beautifully. The praise credits the whole process to its Maker.

phrases.translation: After that you will surely die
phrases.explanation: The verse states the end that follows these beginnings. After all of that, you will surely die, and the commentary explains it as the return to dust from which people were made. The brevity is deliberate, since a single sentence covers what happens to every person who has just been described in the womb. The next verse supplies what death does not end.

phrases.translation: then on the Day of
phrases.explanation: The Day of Judgment is named as the time when the dead are raised, and the commentary explains the resurrection as being brought out of the graves to stand before Allah. The phrase ties the whole passage together, since the One who formed a person from clay and a drop is being credited with forming him again from dust.

phrases.translation: Judgment you will be resurrected
phrases.explanation: Resurrection is stated as a fact that follows death, and the commentary explains the word as being raised from the grave and restored to life. The pairing of death and resurrection in two short verses answers the objection the surah will later report from those who denied it. The argument runs from the first creation to the second, and the passage has just described the first in detail.

phrases.translation: And indeed, We created above you seven levels ˹of heaven˺.
phrases.explanation: Attention moves from the human being to the sky above. Seven levels are described as created above them, and the commentary explains the word as layers, since the Arabs called anything lying above something else a layer. The image is of an ordered structure rather than a single empty space. What is above is presented as no less arranged than what is within the womb.

phrases.translation: We are never unmindful of ˹Our˺ creation
phrases.explanation: The verse then denies that Allah is unmindful of His creation. The commentary explains this as His guarding what is beneath the heavens so that it does not fall upon them and destroy them. The two halves answer each other, since the One who built the structure is the One who keeps it standing.

phrases.translation: We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth.
phrases.explanation: Rain is described as sent down in a measured amount and settled into the earth. The commentary explains that Allah sent the water upon the earth from the sky and caused it to remain there. Measure is the key word, since the gift is not a flood but a quantity that can be stored and used. The verse presents the earth's supply as something deliberately placed rather than merely available.

phrases.translation: And We are surely able to take it away
phrases.explanation: The other side of the gift is the power to withdraw it. The commentary explains that Allah is able to make the water disappear, so that people would perish of thirst, the land would produce nothing, and the livestock would die. The reminder is meant to turn a familiar convenience into a reason for gratitude, since what is given can also be taken away.

phrases.translation: With it We produce for you gardens of palm trees and grapevines,
phrases.explanation: The water's purpose is shown in what it produces. Gardens of palm trees and grapevines are named, and the commentary explains that these two were singled out because they were the foremost fruits of the region, the dates of Medina and the grapes of Taif. The verse reminds the people of blessings they already knew, presenting what was familiar as evidence of a giver.

phrases.translation: in which there are abundant fruits, and from which you may eat
phrases.explanation: The gardens are said to contain abundant fruits, and the commentary notes that the pronoun may refer to the gardens or to the two kinds of plant. Either way the point is that what grows is not merely enough but plentiful. The verse lists what can be eaten, and by naming food it keeps the argument close to daily experience rather than to abstract claims about providence.

phrases.translation: as well as ˹olive˺ trees which grow at Mount Sinai,
phrases.explanation: The olive tree is added to the list, described as growing at Mount Sinai. The commentary explains that the tree stands in apposition to the gardens and that the olive is meant, with the mountain described as one that produces trees. The verse widens the list of provision beyond the two fruits that dominated the region, showing the same water producing different gifts in different places.

phrases.translation: providing oil and a condiment to eat
phrases.explanation: The produce is named as oil and a condiment, and the commentary explains the oil as what the tree yields and the condiment as what eaters use it for. Reciters differed over the reading of the verb for growing, and the commentary treats both readings as sound while preferring the one the majority read. The detail is small and concrete, keeping the argument anchored in daily use.

phrases.translation: And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle,
phrases.explanation: The cattle are presented as a lesson. The commentary explains the lesson as what people learn from them about Allah's favour and power, since nothing He intends escapes Him and nothing He desires is impossible for Him. The word lesson suggests that the animals are meant to be read as evidence rather than merely used, and gratitude follows from understanding what one is looking at.

phrases.translation: from whose bellies We give you ˹milk˺ to drink,
phrases.explanation: The specific gift is milk, described as coming from their bellies, and the commentary notes that it comes forth between the dung and the blood. The detail is unglamorous and deliberate, since nothing about the source suggests purity, yet what emerges is pure drink. The verse invites the hearer to see the production of milk as a sign rather than a fact of nature.

phrases.translation: and in them are many other benefits for you, and from them you may eat
phrases.explanation: The verse adds that there are many benefits in them, naming loads carried and rides taken, and that their flesh provides food. The commentary explains the benefits as the camels that carry loads and are ridden and whose milk is drunk. Provision is thus described across several uses rather than one. What people take from the animals every day is presented as a gift arranged for them in advance.

phrases.translation: And you are carried upon ˹some of˺ them
phrases.explanation: The same animals that provide milk and meat also carry people, and the verse names them beside ships. The commentary explains the sense as being carried on the cattle overland and on the ships by sea. The pairing draws attention to travel as provision in its own right, since movement is what allows a people to live and trade rather than stay where they were born.

phrases.translation: and upon ships
phrases.explanation: Ships are added to the picture, and the commentary explains the sentence as covering carriage on land and sea together. Having spoken of what the animals give as food and drink, the verse ends with what they give as transport. The mention of ships widens the view beyond the desert, so that the argument about provision is not limited to one landscape or one people.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent Noah to his people.
phrases.explanation: Noah is the first messenger named in this sequence, and the surah gives him the same words later messengers will use. Being sent to his own people means he was known to them, not an outsider arriving with a strange claim. The commentary describes the call as an invitation to obedience, to the acknowledgment of Allah's oneness, and to the renunciation of every other object of worship.

phrases.translation: He declared, “O my people! Worship Allah ˹alone˺.
phrases.explanation: The opening of his speech marks the point where the argument begins. Worship is directed to Allah alone because no other being holds any claim to it. The command is not presented as a new invention but as the original relation between the Creator and those He made. Noah addresses them as his own people, which makes the call an appeal from inside the community rather than a demand from outside it.

phrases.translation: You have no god other than Him.
phrases.explanation: These words give the reason behind the command. The commentary explains them as a denial that any object of worship besides Allah could ever be rightly worshipped, so the issue is not which idol is greater but whether idols have any standing before God at all. The line is drawn sharply because the whole dispute with Noah's people turns on this single claim.

phrases.translation: Will you not then fear ˹Him˺?”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a question rather than a threat, asking whether they will not fear the consequence of worshipping something other than Him. The commentary reads the fear as the punishment that follows false worship. Framing it as a question leaves room for the hearers to reconsider while making clear that the warning is real. The same closing appeal returns in the next generation's story.

phrases.translation: But the disbelieving chiefs of his people said ˹to the masses˺,
phrases.explanation: Opposition comes from the chiefs, the notables whose standing gave their words weight among the people, and the verse notes that they disbelieved. Their argument is social before it is theological, since a messenger who is only a man cannot have authority over others like him. The commentary identifies them as the leaders who rejected Allah's oneness and denied Noah, and who then put this reasoning to the ordinary people.

phrases.translation: “This is only a human like you, who wants to be superior to you.
phrases.explanation: Their first objection is that Noah is a human being like them who wants to rise above them and be followed while they remain followers. The complaint concerns status rather than evidence. It assumes that a messenger must belong to a higher order of being, which is exactly the assumption the surah keeps testing. The commentary explains that they accused him of seeking ascendancy over them.

phrases.translation: Had Allah willed, He could have easily sent down angels ˹instead˺.
phrases.explanation: They add that if Allah had wanted to be worshipped alone, He could have sent angels down instead. The commentary spells out the reasoning, that Allah would have sent angels as messengers carrying the call Noah was carrying. The objection treats God's choice of a human messenger as evidence against the message, when the verse presents it as a preference for anything that would spare them from answering to one of their own.

phrases.translation: We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers
phrases.explanation: Their last argument is precedent. What Noah teaches, they say, was never heard among their forefathers, as though unfamiliarity settled the question. The commentary identifies the claim as a denial that anyone before them had been told to worship one God. The surah keeps answering this kind of thinking, because it measures truth by what people already know rather than by what the messenger brings.

phrases.translation: He is simply insane,
phrases.explanation: When argument fails they turn to insult. Calling Noah mad dismisses him without answering him, and it lets them treat his warning as the product of a disturbed mind rather than a claim to be examined. The commentary notes the word used for madness, which in Arabic is linked to the jinn, as though his ideas came from an unseen source that had unseated his reason.

phrases.translation: so bear with him for a while.”
phrases.explanation: To bear with him for a while means to wait him out, tolerating him until some unspecified time settles the matter. The commentary observes that no fixed date is intended, only a vague deferral. It is a convenient way of avoiding a decision, neither accepting the message nor confronting it, while hoping that time will remove the messenger. The surah shows how that delay ended for them.

phrases.translation: Noah prayed, “My Lord! Help me,
phrases.explanation: After a long period of rejection Noah turns to his Lord and asks for help. The commentary describes the call as coming once the matter had endured, ages had passed, and the people persisted in their error. Asking for help is not impatience but the response of a messenger who has done what he can and places the outcome with the One who sent him.

phrases.translation: because they have denied ˹me˺.”
phrases.explanation: The reason he gives is their denial of him, and the commentary ties that denial to what he conveyed of the message and called them to of Allah's oneness. Their rejection was not a verdict on his character but a refusal of the truth he brought. The prayer states the case plainly and asks God to judge between him and a people who would not listen.

phrases.translation: So We inspired him: “Build the Ark under Our ˹watchful˺ Eyes and directions.
phrases.explanation: The answer to Noah's prayer is not rest but work. He is told to build a vessel under Allah's watchful eyes and directions, which the commentary explains as being in God's presence and under His supervision, with the craft itself taught to him by revelation. The command shows the rescue being prepared openly, in the sight of a mocking people, on the strength of God's instruction rather than human calculation.

phrases.translation: Then when Our command comes and the oven bursts ˹with water˺,
phrases.explanation: The sign to begin loading is the coming of Allah's command together with the overflowing of the oven. The commentary takes the command as the decree of punishment on his people, and notes that the exact sense of the oven bursting has been discussed at length elsewhere. The unusual image fixes a moment known to Noah but hidden from everyone else, so boarding begins only when God gives the word.

phrases.translation: take on board a pair from every species along with your family—except those against whom the decree ˹to drown˺ has already been passed.
phrases.explanation: The instruction is to take a pair from every species along with his family, with one exception. The commentary explains the exception as the person against whom the decree of drowning had already passed, and reports identify him as a son of Noah who refused to board. No pleading is allowed for those who did wrong, because the decree is settled. The boat carries a renewed world and leaves the doomed behind.

phrases.translation: And do not plead with Me for those who have done wrong, for they will surely be drowned.”
phrases.explanation: Noah is warned not to plead for the wrongdoers, since their drowning is already decided. The command is severe, and the commentary presents it as Allah's answer to any request that those who disbelieved be spared. It closes the door on appeals that would overturn the decree, and it prepares the reader for the grief of a father whose son is not saved, a scene the Qur'an tells elsewhere.

phrases.translation: Then when you and those with you have settled in the Ark,
phrases.explanation: Once the boat is settled and the danger has passed, the command is to speak. The commentary describes settling as being firmly established aboard, riding high above the water with those of his household who came with him. Thanksgiving is required at the moment of safety, before the new life begins, so that deliverance is credited to Allah rather than to the skill of the builder or the strength of the vessel.

phrases.translation: say, “All praise is for Allah, Who saved us from the wrongdoing people.”
phrases.explanation: The words of thanks credit Allah with saving them from the wrongdoing people. The commentary identifies the wrongdoing here as the worship of other beings alongside God, so the deliverance is moral as much as physical, since the family is carried out of a society that had rejected its Lord. Their rescue also means they are not counted among the wrongdoers, and the sentence keeps that difference before them.

phrases.translation: And pray, “My Lord! Allow me a blessed landing,
phrases.explanation: The next prayer is for the landing. The commentary explains that Noah asks to be brought down at a blessed place after leaving the vessel, and it records that reciters read the word for landing in two ways, one naming a blessed manner of descent and the other a blessed place. Both readings ask for the same thing, that the new beginning should carry God's blessing and not be merely dry ground.

phrases.translation: for You are the best accommodator.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends by naming Allah as the best of those who give a safe landing, since He is the one who brings His servants to rest. The commentary treats this comparison as part of the request itself, not as decoration. The wording keeps the rescued community dependent on the One who saved it, and it turns a simple disembarkation into an act of worship, setting the tone for the testing that follows.

phrases.translation: Surely in this are lessons.
phrases.explanation: The story closes with the statement that it contains lessons, and the commentary explains these as signs for the Prophet's own people, the Quraysh who associated others with God. What happened to Noah's people is presented as evidence of how Allah deals with those who deny His messengers, so the warning reaches an audience that does not consider itself bound by an old story.

phrases.translation: And We ˹always˺ put ˹people˺ to the test
phrases.explanation: The second sentence adds that Allah always tests people. The commentary explains the testing here as the reminders and signs sent before any punishment, giving people the chance to change while there is still time. The destruction is therefore not arbitrary. Each generation is first addressed and warned, and only then held to account for what it did with what it was shown.

phrases.translation: Then We raised another generation after them
phrases.explanation: After the flood the line of humanity continues through other generations, and the surah moves to them without ceremony. The verse establishes that history did not end with the destruction of Noah's people, and that rising generations inherit the same test. The commentary reads it simply as Allah bringing other peoples into existence after them, which prepares for the messenger sent to one of those peoples.

phrases.translation: and sent to them a messenger from among themselves, ˹declaring,˺ “Worship Allah ˹alone˺.
phrases.explanation: The pattern of the previous story repeats. A messenger is raised from among the people themselves, not from outside, and the message opens with the same call to worship Allah alone. The commentary describes him as coming to them with that call and with the rejection of the gods and idols they served. The repetition is deliberate, showing one consistent message delivered to community after community.

phrases.translation: You have no god other than Him.
phrases.explanation: The same ground is stated again, that no object of worship has any claim beside Him. The commentary explains that worship belongs to Him alone, so the many gods of their ancestors have no standing at all. Nothing in the verse appeals to what is new or unfamiliar. It presents the claim as the one that has always been true, and asks why a people who know their own dependence should ignore it.

phrases.translation: Will you not then fear ˹Him˺?”
phrases.explanation: The verse again closes with a question about fear, and the commentary reads it as asking whether they will not fear Allah's punishment while He is the only God they have. The question connects the facts just stated with their conduct. It assumes that recognition should produce reverence, and it treats their failure to fear as a failure to see what their own situation already implies.

phrases.translation: But the chiefs of his people—who disbelieved, denied the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter,
phrases.explanation: The speakers are again the notables, and the verse describes them with three traits before reporting what they said. They rejected faith, they denied that they would meet Allah in the Hereafter, and they had been softened and made insolent by the wealth and ease given to them. The commentary identifies them as the leading men of Thamud, the people to whom Salih was sent, and explains the luxury as abundance that led them to insolence.

phrases.translation: and were spoiled by the worldly luxuries We had provided for them—said ˹to the masses˺,
phrases.explanation: Being spoiled by worldly luxuries is given as a cause, not a decoration. The commentary explains that their livelihood had been widened for them until they grew insolent and transgressed against their Lord. Comfort had made them feel secure, and that feeling shaped how they heard a messenger who warned them of judgement. The verse links their theology to their circumstances, showing how plenty can harden a people against the truth.

phrases.translation: “This is only a human like you.
phrases.explanation: Their objection repeats the one made against Noah, that a messenger is only a human being like those he addresses. The commentary sets out the reasoning behind it, that Allah had favoured Salih with the message while he remained a man who ate and drank as they did, so why had no angel been sent instead? The argument begins from the assumption that guidance must arrive in a form that bypasses human equality.

phrases.translation: He eats what you eat, and drinks what you drink
phrases.explanation: The final observation is meant to make the messenger ordinary and therefore dismissible. He eats what they eat and drinks what they drink, so nothing about him appears to set him apart from them. The commentary takes the words at face value and explains the comparison lying behind them. The surah lets the objection stand as it was spoken, leaving the reader to see that sharing human nature is no argument against a message.

phrases.translation: And if you ˹ever˺ obey a human like yourselves,
phrases.explanation: The chiefs press their case by warning of loss. If the people follow a human being like themselves, they will surrender the standing and superiority they enjoy among the tribes. The commentary explains the loss they fear as being deprived of their share of eminence and elevation in this world. What they call loss is social advantage, which shows that their anxiety is about rank rather than about truth.

phrases.translation: then you would certainly be losers
phrases.explanation: The conclusion is that obedience to a human messenger is ruin, and the commentary reports this as the notables' claim about losing worldly position. The verse sets up the reversal the surah keeps returning to, since those who count themselves winners by holding on to status may be the ones who lose. Measured by the next life, the trade they refuse is the one that would have profited them.

phrases.translation: Does he promise you
phrases.explanation: The question is aimed at the audience rather than at the messenger, inviting them to hear how strange the promise sounds when it is put plainly. Does he promise you that you will be raised? The form of the question expects a denial, and the commentary presents it as the notables placing the claim before the people in order to make it look absurd. The next words show how far they thought the promise went.

phrases.translation: that once you are dead and reduced to dust and bones,
phrases.explanation: The description is deliberately physical. They picture themselves dead, turned to dust, and reduced to bones after the flesh has decayed, and they ask how such remains could leave the graves alive. The commentary explains that the objection concerns the resurrection of the body, which they thought impossible precisely because they could imagine nothing beyond its dissolution. The imagery is meant to make the promise sound like an impossibility.

phrases.translation: you will be brought forth ˹alive˺
phrases.explanation: What they are mocking is the claim that they will be brought out of their graves alive, as they were before death. The commentary notes a grammatical discussion about the repeated word for you, which the reciters and grammarians treated, but the sense remains single and clear. The verse ends on the claim itself, leaving the answer to come from the surah's own argument about the power of Allah.

phrases.translation: Impossible, simply impossible
phrases.explanation: The word used here means far off, and it is repeated for emphasis, as though the promised resurrection were being waved away into the distance. The commentary explains it as the notables declaring that what they were promised will never happen. The repetition gives the dismissal a scornful rhythm, and the surah preserves the tone of it. Rather than offering a reason, they simply announce that the matter is impossible.

phrases.translation: is what you are promised
phrases.explanation: The second half names what is being dismissed, the promise that they would be raised after death. The commentary identifies it as the resurrection the messenger announced. Placing the phrase after the exclamation makes the denial sound decisive, yet the surah treats it as a claim that was never argued. The reader is invited to notice the difference between certainty of tone and strength of evidence.

phrases.translation: There is nothing beyond our worldly life.
phrases.explanation: The claim is that nothing exists beyond the present life, so that the story of a person closes with death. The commentary explains the phrase as a denial of any life other than the one they were living. This is not doubt but a settled conclusion, and it is the foundation on which they reject every warning the messenger brings. The verse gives their view in their own words before it is answered.

phrases.translation: We die, others are born, and none will be resurrected
phrases.explanation: They describe life as a cycle of deaths and births, some dying while others are born, with no return afterwards. The commentary records an early explanation comparing people to crops, one mown down while another sprouts up. The image makes the world look self-renewing and sufficient, and from it they conclude that no one will be raised. The surah later turns that same image of reviving the earth into evidence for resurrection.

phrases.translation: He is no more than a man who has fabricated a lie about Allah,
phrases.explanation: The accusation is that the messenger has invented a lie about Allah, and the commentary ties it to the two claims they found hardest, that there is no god besides Him and that the dead will be raised. Having no answer to the message, they attack the honesty of the one who brought it. The charge is serious, and it shows how completely they had closed the question of whether he might be telling the truth.

phrases.translation: and we will never believe in him.”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a flat refusal to believe him, and the commentary explains it as a refusal to acknowledge him as truthful in what he said about Allah's oneness and about the resurrection. The refusal is stated as a decision rather than a conclusion drawn from evidence. It also marks the point where argument stops, since the next verse reports the messenger turning to his Lord for help.

phrases.translation: The messenger prayed, “My Lord! Help me,
phrases.explanation: This is the same prayer Noah made, and the repetition ties the two stories together. The commentary places it after Salih had despaired of his people believing and after they had declared that they would not believe in him. Turning to Allah at that point is presented as the proper response to rejection, a plea for help against a people who had refused the truth rather than a request for personal vindication.

phrases.translation: because they have denied ˹me˺.”
phrases.explanation: The ground of the prayer is their denial of him. The commentary explains that he asks for help because of what they denied him of the truth he called them to, and because of their hostility toward him. The wording keeps the focus on the message rather than on wounded pride. The manner of help is left unspecified, so the answer that follows comes as a decree from Allah rather than a plan of the messenger's own.

phrases.translation: Allah responded, “Soon they will be truly regretful.”
phrases.explanation: The answer is brief and describes neither the punishment nor its form, only its nearness and its result. They will soon regret, and the commentary explains that only a short while remained before those who denied him would regret their denial, at the moment when the trial came down and repentance could no longer help them. The reply also tells the messenger that his case has been heard, which is what the prayer sought.

phrases.translation: Then the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them with justice,
phrases.explanation: The blast is described as taking them in justice, and the commentary explains that Allah's vengeance came upon them in truth and fairness, because the punishment matched what they had earned by unbelief and by denying His messenger. The wording keeps the disaster from looking arbitrary, since it is a judgement rather than an accident of nature. The surah treats it as the consequence of a decision they had made.

phrases.translation: and We reduced them to rubble.
phrases.explanation: The image of rubble is of debris floating on a flood, the scum from which nothing useful is taken. The commentary records several early explanations, including dead and decayed plant matter and the refuse carried by water, and notes that the point is a comparison showing that they were destroyed and left without use. A people who had been proud becomes the residue of a torrent.

phrases.translation: So away with the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: The closing curse is literally a call for distance, and the commentary reads it as Allah removing the unbelieving people far from Himself by destroying them, because they did not believe in their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and wronged themselves. The verse names them wrongdoers rather than victims. It closes the story as the story of Noah closed, with the same verdict on a people who refused.

phrases.translation: Then We raised other generations after them
phrases.explanation: One line carries the story forward. After the destruction of Thamud another people is brought into existence, and the surah does not linger over the transition. The commentary reads it as Allah bringing forth a different people in their place. The brevity is part of the argument, since it presents the rise and fall of whole communities as a single repeated movement in God's dealings with humanity.

phrases.translation: No people can advance their doom,
phrases.explanation: The verse states that no community can bring its appointed term forward. The commentary explains the term as the destruction appointed for each people, and reads the sentence as a warning to those who thought their respite meant they had escaped. Nothing they do can force that hour to arrive early, however confident they feel and however long their ancestors seemed to last.

phrases.translation: nor can they delay it
phrases.explanation: The second half adds that the term cannot be postponed either. Together the two statements close every exit, so that neither haste nor delay belongs to the people concerned. The commentary applies this to the opponents of the Prophet, telling them that being given time while they disbelieved only carries them to the moment already fixed, after which the pattern seen in earlier communities would follow.

phrases.translation: Then We sent Our messengers in succession:
phrases.explanation: The messengers are sent in succession, one following behind another, and the commentary explains the word as communities receiving messengers in sequence, each following the track of the one before. The image is of a continuous line rather than of isolated episodes. It prepares for the pattern that follows, in which every community in that line repeats the same response to the one sent to it.

phrases.translation: whenever a messenger came to his people, they denied him.
phrases.explanation: The response is uniform. Each community denies its messenger, and the commentary explains that the denial concerns the truth he brought from Allah. The repetition has a cumulative effect, showing that the problem did not lie with one difficult people or one unsuccessful messenger. Something in the hearers kept producing the same refusal, and the surah lets that pattern speak before naming its consequence.

phrases.translation: So We destroyed them, one after the other, reducing them to ˹cautionary˺ tales.
phrases.explanation: The consequence is that they are destroyed one after another, and the commentary describes the destruction as Allah causing one community to follow another into ruin. The verse then says they were turned into tales, which the commentary explains as their becoming a byword repeated among people, used as an illustration of evil rather than of good. Their memory survives only as a warning.

phrases.translation: So away with the people who refuse to believe
phrases.explanation: The passage ends with the same formula used earlier, calling woe upon a people who will not believe. The commentary reads it as a prayer that Allah remove them far away, because they neither believed in Him nor affirmed His messenger. The repeated curse marks the end of a long sequence of warnings. It also sets the stage for the next passage, where the story of Moses begins.

phrases.translation: Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron
phrases.explanation: Moses and his brother Aaron are sent together, which is unusual among the messengers named so far, and the pair are given two kinds of support. The signs are the proofs they will display, and the compelling proof is the authority that leaves no honest excuse for rejection. The commentary identifies their mission as directed to Pharaoh and the leading men of his court, and it explains the signs as the proofs Allah granted them.

phrases.translation: with Our signs and compelling proof
phrases.explanation: The phrase names what accompanied them, and the commentary explains the signs as the miracles Moses was given along with the clear demonstration of his truth. The pairing matters because the brothers were not sent with words alone. The surah presents the confrontation as a contest between an earthly ruler's claims and evidence that no ruler can produce, and the next verses show how that contest was received.

phrases.translation: to Pharaoh and his chiefs,
phrases.explanation: The audience is specified as Pharaoh and his chiefs rather than the people at large, since the court held the power to accept or refuse. The commentary notes that these were the leading men of his people. Addressing the leaders first reflects how the surah has treated the earlier stories, where the notables organise opposition and shape what the ordinary people hear.

phrases.translation: but they behaved arrogantly and were a tyrannical people
phrases.explanation: Their response is arrogance, and the commentary explains that they refused to follow Moses and to believe what he brought from Allah. They are also described as a people who set themselves above others in their land, subjugating the children of Israel and others by force. The verse joins pride in status with the cruelty that grows from it, presenting the two as a single disposition rather than separate faults.

phrases.translation: They argued, “Will we believe in two humans, like ourselves,
phrases.explanation: The objection is again about human equality, but here it has a sharper edge. Two men like ourselves, they say, cannot be believed, and they add that the people of these two are their servants. The commentary explains that the children of Israel were obedient and subservient to them, so the argument is that a nation's low standing disqualifies anyone from it as a messenger.

phrases.translation: whose people are slaves to us?”
phrases.explanation: The word for slaves here carries the sense of those who submit and obey, and the commentary notes that Arabs used it of anyone submissive to a king, as the people of al-Hira were called servants of the Persians. Their question concerns a reversal of rank, whether they should raise above themselves men whose people serve them. Their thinking measures the truth by social position rather than by evidence.

phrases.translation: So they rejected them both,
phrases.explanation: The rejection is stated without argument, and the outcome follows at once. They denied both brothers, and the commentary explains that they were then among those whom Allah destroyed, just as earlier communities that denied their messengers had been destroyed. The pattern already seen with Noah and with Thamud is applied here without further comment, as though the reader should recognise it.

phrases.translation: and ˹so˺ were among those destroyed
phrases.explanation: The phrase among those destroyed places the court of Pharaoh in a line the surah has been drawing since its opening verses. Their end is presented as an instance of the same judgement rather than a unique event, and the plural form keeps the whole court in view, not the king alone. It also prepares for the next verse, which turns from Pharaoh to what Moses was given.

phrases.translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture,
phrases.explanation: The focus shifts from the court to the Scripture given to Moses, and the commentary identifies it as the Torah. The gift is named alongside the mission because the guidance was meant to outlast the confrontation with Pharaoh and to form the community that came out with Moses. What began as a dispute between two brothers and a king ends with a book placed among a people.

phrases.translation: so perhaps his people would be ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: The purpose is stated softly, that his people might be guided. The commentary explains this as the children of Israel being guided by the Scripture and acting on what it contains. The wording does not guarantee the outcome, since guidance is offered as a possibility and the surah later shows how they responded. The verse keeps the gift and the responsibility that comes with it together.

phrases.translation: And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign,
phrases.explanation: The sign here is the pair themselves, the son of Mary and his mother, and the commentary explains that they are a proof of Allah's power to create a body without a father. The verse says nothing about how the child was conceived, only that the two of them together constitute evidence. It is the same kind of argument the surah has used for the creation of the first human being.

phrases.translation: and gave them refuge on high ground—a ˹suitable˺ place for rest with flowing water
phrases.explanation: The second half provides shelter. They are given refuge on elevated ground described as a suitable place for rest with flowing water, and the commentary explains the high ground as raised land standing above its surroundings. It also records disagreement over which place is meant, with suggestions including a spot in Palestine, Damascus, Egypt, and Jerusalem, and it settles on the description rather than on any one name.

phrases.translation: O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously.
phrases.explanation: The address is to messengers in the plural, and the commentary notes that it is spoken to Jesus, with the plural used in the way Arabic sometimes addresses one person as a class. The command to eat what is good and lawful ties daily food to the prophetic office, since what sustains the messenger should be pure when the message itself demands purity of the one who carries it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, I fully know what you do
phrases.explanation: Righteous action follows lawful food, so the two halves of the command belong together. The commentary explains that Allah knows every deed, that nothing of them is hidden from Him, and that He will repay each person fully for what was done. Mention of knowledge is not a passing remark but a reason for effort, since no action goes unrecorded, and it closes the instruction with accountability.

phrases.translation: Surely this religion of yours is ˹only˺ one,
phrases.explanation: The religion given to the messengers is one, and the commentary explains the word for community here as also meaning the religion itself and the body of those who follow it. Against the many sects that will appear, the verse states a single origin. Reciters differ over how the sentence is read grammatically, which the commentary discusses at length, but the meaning of unity is unaffected.

phrases.translation: and I am your Lord, so fear Me ˹alone˺
phrases.explanation: The sentence closes with Allah declaring Himself their Lord and commanding them to fear Him alone. The commentary explains the fear as obedience, so that they may be safe from His punishment. Placed immediately after the statement of unity, the command shows why division is so serious, since what is at stake is not merely agreement among people but loyalty to the One who sent them.

phrases.translation: Yet the people have divided it into different sects,
phrases.explanation: The people are described as dividing their religion into portions, and the commentary records two ways of reading the word behind this, one meaning books and the other meaning fragments, as of iron. On the first reading each group followed a book of its own, such as Jews holding to the Torah and Christians to the Gospel. The division is doctrinal, made by choosing one revelation and refusing the rest.

phrases.translation: each rejoicing in what they have
phrases.explanation: The verse adds that each party rejoices in what it has. The commentary explains this as each community delighting in the religion and the books it chose for itself, convinced that the truth rested with them alone. The rejoicing is the symptom rather than the cure, since pleasure in one's own position can make a person stop asking whether the position is true.

phrases.translation: So leave them ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The command to leave them is addressed to the Prophet, and the commentary explains it as a directive to turn from those who had divided their religion into books. It sets a limit on controversy with people who have stopped listening, and it is not an approval of what they believe. The next verse explains why their confidence was misplaced, since the delay was a respite and not an endorsement.

phrases.translation: in their heedlessness for a while
phrases.explanation: Their state is named heedlessness, which the commentary explains as error and blindness. The words for a while limit how long that condition lasts, and the commentary identifies the limit as the appointed term when punishment arrives. The phrasing holds two truths together, that they are genuinely lost and that their being left alone is temporary. Both are meant to sober the reader as much as to describe them.

phrases.translation: Do they think,
phrases.explanation: The question challenges a conclusion they had quietly reached, that wealth and children were proof of Allah's favour. The commentary frames it as asking whether these factions supposed that what they were given in this fleeting life was being rushed to them as a reward. The verse exposes the assumption that anyone who prospers must be approved, which the stories of the destroyed peoples have already contradicted.

phrases.translation: since We provide them with wealth and children
phrases.explanation: What they are given is described as provision of wealth and sons, the two things they valued most. The commentary explains that being supplied with these was not a sign of nearness to Allah but a granting of time, a gradual leading toward ruin. The verse reinterprets prosperity without denying that it comes from Allah, and it turns what looked like an argument for their security into a warning.

phrases.translation: that We hasten to ˹honour˺ them ˹with˺ all kinds of good?
phrases.explanation: The question is completed here. Do wealth and children mean that Allah is hurrying good things to them? The commentary records early explanations that the verse addresses the Quraysh and that the hastening means increasing their good and granting them respite. Read with the previous verse, it shows a mistake in which material ease is taken for the reward that belongs to the next life.

phrases.translation: No! They are not aware
phrases.explanation: The answer is a flat denial followed by its explanation. No, they are not aware, which the commentary ties to their failure to realise that the support they received was a respite rather than a reward. Their mistake is not a lack of intelligence but a lack of perception about what their own condition means. The verse ends there, leaving the reader to draw the conclusion.

phrases.translation: Surely those who tremble in awe of their Lord
phrases.explanation: Fear here is not a passing emotion but a settled awe that keeps a person careful. The commentary explains it as dread of Allah's punishment that drives those who feel it to constant obedience and to seeking His pleasure. The verse begins a description that runs through the next four verses, so the trembling is the root of everything that follows. It also sets the tone for the contrast with the careless that comes later.

phrases.translation: and who believe in the revelations of their Lord
phrases.explanation: Belief is described as affirming the signs of Allah's book and the proofs He set before people. The commentary keeps the phrase broad, so that the signs include what is recited and what is seen. Placed after fear and before the rejection of partners, belief here is not a single moment of assent but a continuing response to what Allah keeps showing. It is the inward side of the obedience just described.

phrases.translation: and who associate none with their Lord
phrases.explanation: The verse names the one thing that spoils worship, which is associating anything with Allah. The commentary explains it as keeping worship pure for Him and giving no partner a share in it, whether an idol, an image, or the wish to be seen by people. Even a good deed can be spoiled by wanting an audience, so the commentary adds that deeds are rendered for His countenance alone, with obedience turned to Him above all else.

phrases.translation: and who do whatever ˹good˺ they do with their hearts fearful,
phrases.explanation: The giving described is the obligatory alms, and the commentary explains it as the share Allah fixed in a person's wealth being handed to those entitled to it. What makes the verse striking is the state of the giver at the moment of giving. These are people who do good and are afraid, not people who feel their record is settled. Their generosity is real, and so is their unease about whether it will be accepted.

phrases.translation: ˹knowing˺ that they will return to their Lord—
phrases.explanation: The fear is tied to the return to Allah rather than to doubt about His mercy. The commentary records a report in which the Prophet is asked whether the verse means those who sin and fear, and he answers that it means the one who fasts, prays, and gives alms while afraid it will not be accepted. An early saying adds that the believer joins good deeds with fear, while the hypocrite joins evil deeds with a sense of safety.

phrases.translation: it is they who race to do good deeds,
phrases.explanation: The description ends where it began, with action. These are the people who strive in good works and seek nearness to Allah through obedience, and the verse calls them foremost. The racing image suggests that goodness is not merely done but pursued, with effort and with a wish to be early in it. It follows naturally from the fear just described, since a person who takes the return seriously does not delay.

phrases.translation: always taking the lead
phrases.explanation: The commentary records two explanations of their being foremost. One is that happiness had already been decreed for them with Allah, and the other concerns the good deeds themselves, that they go forward in them. It prefers the first, so that Allah's prior decree and their own racing are held together rather than opposed. The verse honours both the divine appointment and the human effort that answers it.

phrases.translation: We never require of any soul more than what it can afford.
phrases.explanation: The verse sets a limit on obligation. No soul is asked to carry more than it can bear, and the commentary explains this as the reason the laws given suit those addressed. It is a statement of mercy placed directly after the description of people racing in good deeds, so that zeal is not mistaken for a demand that people exhaust themselves or despair over what they cannot manage.

phrases.translation: And with Us is a record which speaks the truth.
phrases.explanation: The record is described as speaking the truth, and the commentary explains it as a register of every deed, good and evil, kept with Allah. It is pictured as a witness that states what happened without addition or omission. Since a truthful record is the foundation of a fair reckoning, the phrase prepares for the final assurance. Nothing here depends on memory or on the account a person gives of himself.

phrases.translation: None will be wronged
phrases.explanation: The closing words name the outcome, that no one will be wronged. The commentary explains the wronging in two directions, that no sin is added to the evildoer which he did not commit, and no good deed is taken from the doer of good so that his reward shrinks. The statement is short and complete, and it ends the discussion of fear and effort with a promise that nothing done will be lost or exaggerated.

phrases.translation: But the hearts of those ˹who disbelieve˺ are oblivious to ˹all of˺ this,
phrases.explanation: The verse turns from the believers to those who disbelieve, and the contrast is between sight and blindness. Their hearts are described with a word meaning flooded or submerged, and the commentary explains it as a covering over the heart so that the warnings, lessons, and proofs of the Book do not reach it. The same revelations that guide others find no place in them, and the reason is not a lack of information.

phrases.translation: and they have other ˹evil˺ deeds, opposite to this, in which they are engrossed
phrases.explanation: They are not merely ignorant, since they also have deeds of another kind in which they are engrossed. The commentary explains these as sins, acts Allah does not accept, in contrast to the deeds of those who believe and fear Him. One report describes them as deeds they have not yet done but will do. The verse presents a whole life pointed elsewhere, busy with what keeps the heart from turning back.

phrases.translation: But as soon as We seize their elite with torment,
phrases.explanation: The elite here are the affluent and powerful among the Quraysh, and the commentary explains the word as the great ones, the comfortable and dissolute. When punishment reaches them, their first response is not reflection but noise. The verse marks the moment when confidence collapses, and it locates that moment in the seizure of those whose ease had made them leaders in denial. Their influence was the reason others followed them.

phrases.translation: they start to cry for help
phrases.explanation: The crying out is described with a word for the bellowing of a bull, a raw and helpless sound rather than a considered prayer. The commentary records that early explanations applied it to the day of Badr, when the leading men were struck with the sword, and to the despair of those seized. The picture is deliberately undignified, the proud reduced to howling, and it prepares for the answer that follows.

phrases.translation: ˹They will be told,˺ “Do not cry for help today.
phrases.explanation: The answer refuses the cry before it can grow into a plea. Do not cry today, they are told, because the day for asking has passed and the punishment has already come down. The commentary explains that wailing will not help and will turn aside nothing of Allah's anger. That finality is the point of the line, and it explains why the earlier verses laid such stress on heeding the message while there was time.

phrases.translation: Surely you will never be saved from Us
phrases.explanation: The second half states that no help will come from Allah. The commentary explains it as a declaration that they will not be saved from the punishment that has fallen and that nothing will deliver them from it. The words are addressed to them directly, so the sentence is part of their rebuke rather than a report about them. Mercy was available before, and what remains now is the consequence of having refused it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, My revelations were recited to you,
phrases.explanation: The reason for the refusal is given next. The revelations had been recited to them, so the warning had reached them in plain words. The commentary explains these as the verses of Allah's book, recited while they were present to hear. Their failure was therefore not a lack of access. What the verse records is a people who had the message in front of them and treated it as something to be avoided.

phrases.translation: but you used to back away ˹in disgust˺
phrases.explanation: Their response is described as backing away in disgust, an image of someone retreating from what he has just heard. The commentary notes the Arabic idiom of turning back on one's heels, used of anyone who returns the way he came. The phrase shows that they did not merely fail to accept the recitation but actively withdrew from it, and that withdrawal is now presented as the ground of their sentence.

phrases.translation: boasting of the Sacred House,
phrases.explanation: The charge is that they were arrogant about the Sacred House, and the commentary explains the boast as the claim that no one would overcome them because they were its residents. Their privilege as guardians of the sanctuary had become a guarantee they trusted instead of the obedience the sanctuary called for. The verse names that misplaced confidence as part of what they are held to account for.

phrases.translation: and babbling ˹nonsense about the Quran˺ by night.”
phrases.explanation: The last accusation is night talk, and the commentary explains it as gatherings after dark where they spoke poetry, soothsaying, and other things they did not know. Reciters read the final word in two ways, one meaning that they turned away and forsook the truth, the other that they babbled nonsense about the Qur'an. Both readings describe the same habit of filling the night with speech that pushed revelation aside.

phrases.translation: Is it because they have never contemplated the Word ˹of Allah˺?
phrases.explanation: The verse offers a series of possible reasons for rejection, and the first is that they never reflected on the recitation itself. The commentary explains the question as asking whether they had pondered Allah's revelation so as to see the lessons and proofs set out in it. The reproach is precise, since the message was available and thinking about it had simply not been done.

phrases.translation: Or ˹because˺ there has come to them something that did not come to their forefathers
phrases.explanation: The second possibility is stranger, that they turned away because something had come to them which their forefathers never received. The commentary notes that messengers and books had in fact come to the earlier generations, so the objection does not hold. One report turns the question around and asks whether what reached them was not precisely what had never reached their forefathers. Either way, novelty is no argument against a message.

phrases.translation: Or ˹because˺ they failed to recognize their Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The next question turns from the message to the messenger. Did they fail to recognise him, so that they then denied him? The commentary explains that they knew Muhammad to be truthful and trustworthy and living among them, which makes the denial harder to account for. The verse exposes a gap between what they knew of the man and how they treated what he brought.

phrases.translation: and so they denied him
phrases.explanation: The denial is described as following from a failure to recognise, and the commentary presses the point by asking how they could reject someone whose honesty they had long relied on. Nothing in the verse suggests they thought him a stranger. The difficulty is that they knew him too well to claim ignorance, and that familiarity had not helped them accept the message.

phrases.translation: Or ˹because˺ they say, “He is insane?”
phrases.explanation: The last of these questions is the accusation of madness. The commentary explains it as the claim that Muhammad spoke without meaning, in words that could not be understood. It then answers the charge from the content itself, since what he brought was coherent wisdom whose correctness could not be hidden from anyone of sound understanding. A madman raves, while this recitation holds together.

phrases.translation: In fact, he has come to them with the truth,
phrases.explanation: The reply states simply that he has brought them the truth, and the commentary draws out how completely that reverses the accusation. Truth is the opposite of what is confused and meaningless, so the charge collapses once the message is actually heard. The verse does not argue further, because the claim stands or falls on the content. It places the recitation itself before the reader as the evidence.

phrases.translation: but most of them are resentful of the truth
phrases.explanation: The verse then names the real obstacle. Most of them resent the truth, and the commentary explains that they knew he was truthful and that his call was right, but they would not submit to it out of envy, hostility, and arrogance. The problem is therefore in the will rather than in the mind, and that analysis shapes the verses that follow.

phrases.translation: Had the truth followed their desires,
phrases.explanation: The verse imagines what would happen if revelation were shaped by human preference. Should the truth follow their desires, the whole order of the heavens and the earth would collapse. The commentary explains that creation stands only by the truth, so a world governed by appetite could not hold together. The argument is not that their wishes are unpopular but that they are incapable of sustaining anything.

phrases.translation: the heavens, the earth, and all those in them would have certainly been corrupted.
phrases.explanation: The corruption is cosmic in scope, reaching the heavens, the earth, and everything in them. The commentary adds that this follows from their ignorance of consequences, since they neither know what serves the ordering of affairs nor what harms it, and most of them prefer falsehood to truth. The verse treats their demands not as a private preference but as a proposal for how the world should be run.

phrases.translation: In fact, We have brought them ˹the means to˺ their glory, but they turn away from it
phrases.explanation: In fact, what has come to them is not a loss but their own glory and reminder. The commentary records two readings of that word, one meaning the clarification of truth sent down in the Qur'an and the other meaning honour, since the revelation honoured them by coming to a man from among themselves. The two senses are close, since the same book instructs them and elevates them, and they turn from it anyway.

phrases.translation: Or ˹is it because˺ you ˹O Prophet˺ are asking them for tribute?
phrases.explanation: The next question asks whether the messenger is asking them for payment. The commentary explains that he sought no tribute in return for the counsel and truth he brought, and that he had been told to say that he asked no reward for it. The suggestion is raised only to be dismissed, since a demand for money would have given them a reason to hold back from listening.

phrases.translation: But the reward of your Lord is best, for He is the Best Provider
phrases.explanation: The answer is that the reward of Allah is better for him than anything they could pay. The commentary explains this as the recompense for carrying out the command and seeking His pleasure, and it names Allah as the best of providers, the one who gives both wages and provision. The verse closes the question of motive by showing that the messenger's interest lay entirely with the One who sent him.

phrases.translation: And surely you are calling them
phrases.explanation: The verse states what the messenger is doing. He calls them to the straight path, which the commentary identifies as the religion of submission, a way with no crookedness in it. The claim is simple and puts the emphasis on the invitation rather than on the resistance it meets. Everything in the surrounding verses is meant to show that the way on offer lacks nothing the hearers need.

phrases.translation: to the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: The phrase names the destination of the call, and the commentary describes it as the straight way without deviation, the religion Allah approved for His servants. Calling it straight is a claim about direction rather than about ease, since a straight road may still be hard to walk. The verse leaves the hearers to decide whether the path they are on leads where they think it does.

phrases.translation: but those who disbelieve in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The next verse explains why the call is refused. Those who disbelieve in the Hereafter are described as deviating from the path, and the commentary explains the image as turning aside from the lofty road of truth. The connection is deliberate, since a person who does not expect a reckoning has little reason to accept guidance that leads to one. Denial of the meeting with Allah changes how the road looks.

phrases.translation: are certainly deviating from that Path
phrases.explanation: The deviation is not a small slip but a settled turning away from the way Allah approved for His servants. The commentary explains the Arabic image as stepping aside from a road, the same verb used of someone who leaves a path he was travelling. The verse keeps two ideas together, that the path is straight and that the reason some leave it is that they disbelieve where it leads.

phrases.translation: ˹Even˺ if We had mercy on them and removed their affliction,
phrases.explanation: The verse grants a hypothetical and then reports what it would prove. If Allah had mercy on them and lifted the affliction they were suffering, which the commentary identifies as famine, drought, and the exhaustion of hunger, they would still have persisted in their transgression. Relief would not have produced gratitude. The test was not the hardship itself but what they did with it.

phrases.translation: they would still persist in their transgression, wandering blindly
phrases.explanation: Their persistence is described as wandering blindly, and the commentary explains the image as moving to and fro without direction. They would not have been led back by comfort any more than by hunger, because the problem lay in their obstinacy toward their Lord. That closes off the excuse that circumstances were to blame, since what they needed was not easier conditions but a change of heart.

phrases.translation: And We have already seized them with torment,
phrases.explanation: The next verse reports what had already happened. They were seized with punishment, and the commentary describes drought striking their land, their livelihood narrowing, and their leaders killed with the sword. Despite all of that they did not submit to their Lord. The warning had been given in experience as well as in words, and it still did not produce humility.

phrases.translation: but they never humbled themselves to their Lord,
phrases.explanation: The verse names submission and humble appeal as the two things missing. The commentary explains submission as complying with Allah's command and prohibition and turning toward obedience, and appeal as lowering oneself before Him in supplication. Neither took place. A report ties the verse to the drought that struck the Quraysh after the Prophet invoked a curse against them, when they came asking him to pray for relief.

phrases.translation: nor did they ˹submissively˺ appeal ˹to Him˺
phrases.explanation: The final phrase sharpens the failure by naming the appeal they never made. The commentary explains it as not humbling themselves before Him, and it says nothing about what they offered in its place. The verse records a silence where pleading should have been. It also prepares for the next verse, in which the door they refused to approach is opened for them in a way they cannot bear.

phrases.translation: But as soon as We open for them a gate of severe punishment,
phrases.explanation: The image shifts to a gate being opened, and the commentary records disagreement about which gate is meant. Some explanations name armed conflict, so that they were killed at Badr. The common point is that the opening is not relief but a new and harder phase. What had been hardship before becomes severe punishment, and the verse marks the end of the period in which they were given time.

phrases.translation: they will be utterly desperate
phrases.explanation: The response to that opening is despair, and the commentary explains it as grief and remorse over what they did in the past, at a moment when repentance no longer helps. The proud people who had laughed at warnings are left without a course of action. The surah closes this section as it closed the stories of the earlier communities, with the collapse of those who would not turn back.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who created for you hearing, sight, and intellect.
phrases.explanation: The argument moves from what the hearers already possess to what they doubt. Hearing, sight, and understanding are named as gifts Allah created for them, and the commentary draws the conclusion that the One who first brought these faculties into existence is not unable to raise a person after death. The verse appeals to the equipment of their own bodies as evidence of the power they were questioning.

phrases.translation: ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks
phrases.explanation: The complaint is not that they gave no thanks at all but that they gave very little. The commentary reads the words as addressed to those who denied the resurrection, telling them that their gratitude for hearing, sight, and understanding fell far short of what these gifts deserved. Ingratitude and denial are joined here, since a person who credited the Giver would not find the promise of revival so hard.
