phrases.translation: And He is the One Who has dispersed you ˹all˺ over the earth,
phrases.explanation: From the senses the verse moves outward to the spread of humanity across the earth. Being dispersed is presented as an act of Allah, and the commentary explains it as His creating people upon the earth and placing them in different lands. The same power that scattered them is the power that can gather them, and the verse makes that gathering the counterpart of the scattering.

phrases.translation: and to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered
phrases.explanation: The second half states where the dispersal ends. To Him you will all be gathered, and the commentary explains this as being raised from the graves to the place of reckoning after death. The word all carries the argument, since a promise to gather everyone cannot be defeated by numbers or by distance. What was scattered deliberately can be collected deliberately, and the verse leaves no middle ground.

phrases.translation: And He is the One Who gives life and causes death,
phrases.explanation: Life and death are named as acts of Allah, and the commentary explains the giving of life as bringing a person to life after the drop of seed by breathing the spirit into him. Death is then described as His act as well, following the life He granted. The pairing is the point, since the One who controls both ends of a life is not limited by either of them.

phrases.translation: and to Him belongs the alternation of the day and night.
phrases.explanation: The alternation of day and night is also attributed to Him, and the commentary explains that He is the One who has made each distinct from the other, so that one gives way to the other in order. The ordinary experience of every day is offered as evidence, an unchanging pattern of endings and beginnings that nobody attributes to chance. It is the same reasoning the surah used about rain reviving the earth.

phrases.translation: Will you not then understand
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with a question, asking whether they will not understand. The commentary explains the challenge as asking whether those who see Allah create from nothing cannot see that He is able to give life to the dead after decay and to create again what He had destroyed. The question is meant to be answered by the reader, since the evidence has been placed in plain sight.

phrases.translation: But they ˹just˺ say what their predecessors said
phrases.explanation: Instead of drawing a lesson from these signs, the polytheists simply repeated what earlier nations had said. The commentary explains that they reflected on neither the proofs of Allah's power nor the indications set before them, and produced instead the same objections their predecessors had made. The verse is short and damning, since it shows the response as inherited rather than reasoned.

phrases.translation: They said, “Once we are dead and reduced to dust and bones,
phrases.explanation: Their inherited objection is the familiar one. Once we are dead, reduced to dust and bones, will we really be raised? The commentary expands the picture of decay, with the body dissolved and the bones stripped of flesh. The question is framed to sound impossible, and it rests on the assumption that death is a final condition rather than a stage within the power of the One who made them.

phrases.translation: will we really be resurrected
phrases.explanation: The second half delivers the expected answer, that they considered resurrection beyond possibility. The commentary notes the emphatic form of the question, which expects a denial, and reads it as the claim that such a return could never happen. What makes the objection so persistent in this surah is that it is always stated as obvious rather than argued, and the surrounding verses keep answering it with evidence.

phrases.translation: We have already been promised this, as well as our forefathers earlier.
phrases.explanation: Their second argument is tradition. They say the promise had already been made to them and to their fathers before them, and nothing came of it. The commentary explains that earlier peoples had indeed been promised by men claiming to be messengers, yet these objectors had never seen the promise fulfilled. The reasoning treats delay as disproof, which is exactly the assumption the surah has exposed in earlier passages.

phrases.translation: This is nothing but ancient fables!”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the charge that this is nothing but ancient fables. The commentary explains the phrase as referring to tales the earlier peoples wrote down, reports with no foundation in truth. Calling revelation a story is a way of placing it among things nobody expects to check. The accusation also explains why argument had failed, since a person who treats a claim as fiction does not examine it.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “To whom belong the earth and all those on it,
phrases.explanation: The questioning changes direction. Instead of defending the resurrection, the verse asks the objectors to say who owns the earth and everyone on it. The commentary explains that the question is put to those who deny the Hereafter, and that it is framed to draw out an admission they cannot avoid. It begins a short sequence of such questions, each relying on knowledge they already had.

phrases.translation: if you ˹really˺ know?”
phrases.explanation: The question ends with a condition, if you really know, which turns the challenge back on the hearers. The commentary notes that they will admit the ownership belongs to Allah, since nothing else was conceivable to them. Once that is granted the rest of the argument follows, because the One who owns everything disposes of it as He wills, including its ending and its restoration.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “To Allah!”
phrases.explanation: They answer at once, and the answer is the one they had always believed. The commentary notes the admission that the earth and all upon it belong to Allah as His possession, above everything else and apart from it. The verse lets them state their own position, which makes the next words a rebuke rather than an argument. What they had just conceded was enough to settle the question against them.

phrases.translation: Say, “Why are you not then mindful?”
phrases.explanation: The reply asks why they are not mindful, and the commentary explains the question as an appeal to take heed of what their own answer implies. If Allah was able to create all of this at the beginning, He is able to bring the dead to life and to restore them as complete beings after decay. The verse treats that conclusion as obvious once the premise is granted.

phrases.translation: ˹And˺ ask ˹them˺, “Who is the Lord of the seven heavens
phrases.explanation: The next question scales the same argument upward, asking who is the Lord of the seven heavens. The commentary explains the seven heavens as the layered structures above, and the question is again designed to reach an admission they already held. The pattern is deliberate, moving step by step through what they acknowledged in order to expose what they denied in practice.

phrases.translation: and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?”
phrases.explanation: The second half adds the Mighty Throne, described in the commentary as the throne that encompasses all of this. The addition lifts the question from the created world to the seat of authority over it. Having reached the highest thing they could name, the verse then asks whether they will fear the One who owns it, which is the practical consequence of the answer they were about to give.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “Allah.”
phrases.explanation: Their answer is a single word, Allah, and the commentary records a difference among reciters over how it is read, with some supplying the preposition and others following the written text without it. Both readings were accepted as sound and close in meaning, and the commentary prefers the one matching the codices of the cities. The variation does not touch the admission itself.

phrases.translation: Say, “Will you not then fear ˹Him˺?”
phrases.explanation: The question that follows turns their answer into a charge. If Allah is Lord of the heavens and the Throne, why do they not fear Him? The commentary explains the fear as dread of His punishment for disbelieving Him and denying His message and the message of His messenger. The verse again moves from an agreed premise to a conclusion about conduct, and it does so in the fewest possible words.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them also,˺ “In Whose Hands is the authority over all things,
phrases.explanation: The third question is the widest of them. It asks who holds the authority over all things, the one in whose hands are the treasuries of everything. The commentary explains the phrase as dominion over all affairs, the point the earlier questions had established, now stated in its most comprehensive form. Nothing is left outside the scope of the ownership they are being asked to acknowledge.

phrases.translation: protecting ˹all˺ while none can protect against Him,
phrases.explanation: Protection is then described in a way that belongs to Allah alone. He protects whom He wills, and no one can protect against Him, which the commentary explains as the impossibility of resisting the harm He decides to send. The verse closes with the same condition, if you really know, which reminds them that they are not being told anything new. Their own sense of who holds power is being used to correct them.

phrases.translation: if you ˹really˺ know?”
phrases.explanation: The final clause is the question that has been waiting behind the others. If they truly know the answer, then their knowledge is not in doubt, only their use of it. The commentary treats the words as an appeal to what they already affirm about Allah's sovereignty. The verse therefore asks nothing new of them except that they follow their own admission to its conclusion.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “Allah.”
phrases.explanation: They answer as before, and the commentary notes that they will acknowledge that dominion over all things belongs to Allah. The admission is complete, since nothing in the question leaves room for a partner. The sequence has now established that they accept Allah as owner, as lord of the heavens, and as holder of authority, and the next words ask how their conduct can be reconciled with that.

phrases.translation: Say, “How are you then so deluded?”
phrases.explanation: The final question asks how they can be deluded, and the commentary explains the image of sorcery, in which a thing is shown as other than it really is. The point is that falsehood has been presented to them as truth, turning them from acknowledging what their own answers concede. The verse names the gap between their knowledge and their worship, and it treats that gap as a kind of bewitchment rather than a reasonable position.

phrases.translation: In fact, We have brought them the truth,
phrases.explanation: The passage ends with a verdict. In fact, Allah has brought them the truth, and the commentary identifies this as the religion with which the Prophet was sent, that none but Allah may be worshipped. Set against the answers they had just given, the statement shows that revelation agrees with what they already knew. What they had added to that knowledge was not evidence but invention.

phrases.translation: and they are certainly liars
phrases.explanation: The last words call them liars, and the commentary explains the lie as what they ascribed to Allah, whether a child or a partner. The verse is blunt because the argument has already been made three times and they had conceded every premise. There is nothing left to discuss except the difference between what they knew and what they said, and the surah then turns to state the truth about Allah directly.

phrases.translation: Allah has never had ˹any˺ offspring, nor is there any god besides Him.
phrases.explanation: The verse denies two claims at once, that Allah has a child and that any god exists beside Him. The commentary notes that the denial covers eternity as well as the beginning of creation, so that no partner is imagined at any point. The wording is compact and settles the matter before any argument is offered, because what is denied here is not a detail about God but a distortion of what He is.

phrases.translation: Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created,
phrases.explanation: The second clause describes what would follow. Each god would take what he had created and keep it for himself, which the commentary reads as each deity setting himself apart with his own creation. The shape of the argument is that a divided divinity would produce a divided world.

phrases.translation: and they would have tried to dominate one another.
phrases.explanation: The contention is then stated plainly. They would have tried to dominate one another, and the commentary explains this as each seeking to exalt himself over the rest, with the strong overcoming the weak. A world with several claimants to divinity would be at war at its foundations, which contradicts the ordered creation everyone can see. That contradiction is what makes the denial of partners more than an assertion.

phrases.translation: Glorified is Allah above what they claim
phrases.explanation: The verse ends by declaring Allah glorified above what they claim. The commentary lists the claims in view, that He has a child, that He has an associate, or that something beside Him shares His eternity. The declaration of glory is the fitting response to what has just been shown to be impossible. It also leaves the reader with the greatness of Allah rather than with the smallness of the argument.

phrases.translation: ˹He is the˺ Knower of the seen and unseen.
phrases.explanation: Allah is described as the Knower of what is hidden and what is witnessed, which the commentary explains as covering what creatures cannot see or perceive as well as what they can. The title is placed here to answer claims made without knowledge, since the One who knows everything is in a position to judge what is said about Him. The commentary also discusses how the word is read and prefers the nominative.

phrases.translation: Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him˺
phrases.explanation: The verse then declares Him exalted above what they associate with Him. The commentary explains this as Allah being far removed from any partner and from the attributes the polytheists invented. The two halves work together, since the One whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing needs no correction from those who speak out of ignorance. The passage is not merely refuting them but stating what Allah is in Himself.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord!
phrases.explanation: The verse opens with a command to speak, and what follows is put in the form of a prayer. Addressing Allah as My Lord places the messenger before the One who controls what he is asking about. The instruction to say it also makes the prayer a model for those who hear it, since the words are preserved for recitation rather than left as a private moment.

phrases.translation: Should You show me what they are threatened with
phrases.explanation: The prayer is conditional, asking what to seek if the punishment promised to the polytheists is shown to him. The commentary explains the request as asking not to perish with those Allah destroys, and to be saved from His wrath. Framing it as a condition covers what may or may not come to pass, so the prayer is ready either way. It teaches the believer where to turn when destruction falls.

phrases.translation: then, my Lord, do not count me among the wrongdoing people.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer continues with the request itself. Do not count me among the wrongdoing people, which the commentary explains as asking to be spared from punishment and wrath and to be made one of those with whom Allah is pleased. The commentary also notes the grammar of the sentence, where calling upon the Lord falls between the condition and its answer. The effect is a request that depends entirely on Allah's decision.

phrases.translation: We are indeed able to show you what We have threatened them with
phrases.explanation: The verse reassures the messenger that the delay is not weakness. Allah is able to show him what was threatened against them, and the commentary explains this as the hastening of punishment upon the polytheists. The deferral serves a purpose, so that the book may reach its appointed term. The verse gives assurance of power and a reason for patience at once, and their denial is not to grieve him.

phrases.translation: Respond to evil with what is best.
phrases.explanation: The command is to answer evil with what is better. The commentary explains it as turning away from the ignorant among the polytheists, pardoning them, and enduring their persecution, and it notes that this was the instruction before the command to fight. Responding well does not mean approving what was done, but refusing to let it dictate the response. The verse addresses the messenger's own conduct under provocation.

phrases.translation: We know well what they claim
phrases.explanation: The second sentence gives the reason such restraint is possible. Allah knows best what they say about Him and about His messenger, and the commentary explains that He will repay them for the lies and slanders. That knowledge takes the pressure off the person being insulted, since nothing said is lost and nothing goes unrecorded. The command to forgive rests on the assurance that justice is not absent.

phrases.translation: And say, “My Lord! I seek refuge in You
phrases.explanation: The prayer turns to the inner side of the same struggle. Refuge is sought from the temptations of the devils, and the commentary explains the word as a throttling grip or pressure, the kind of squeezing that provokes a person toward evil. The image is not of open attack but of a constriction that pushes someone off course. Seeking refuge is therefore an admission that human resolve needs protection from outside itself.

phrases.translation: from the temptations of the devils
phrases.explanation: The verse names the source of danger as the devils, and the commentary ties the word to promptings rather than to visible harm. What is feared is influence over the mind and the will, the sort of pressure that can make an evil act seem reasonable. The prayer stands in the same passage as the command to answer evil with good, suggesting that the hardest battles are fought within the person who is provoked.

phrases.translation: And I seek refuge in You, my Lord,
phrases.explanation: The prayer adds a further request, that they not even come near. The commentary explains it as asking that the devils not be present with him in his affairs. Not being harmed is thus not enough, since nearness itself is treated as the beginning of harm. The second request is more cautious than the first, and it shows how seriously the danger of influence is taken.

phrases.translation: that they ˹even˺ come near me.”
phrases.explanation: Asking that they not come near marks the limit the worshipper wants set. The commentary explains the presence of the devils as their attending a person in his affairs, so the prayer is for distance rather than for a contest. That preference for distance over confrontation is itself a form of wisdom. It also fits the passage, where the response to hostility is restraint rather than retaliation.

phrases.translation: When death approaches any of them, they cry,
phrases.explanation: The scene shifts to the moment of death. When it approaches one of them, the same people who denied the resurrection begin to plead. The commentary explains the cry as arising from the enormity of what he sees of the punishment awaiting him, together with remorse over the obedience he neglected. The request to be sent back is not a request for knowledge but for another chance.

phrases.translation: “My Lord! Let me go back
phrases.explanation: The plea itself is for a return to the world, and the commentary explains it simply as asking to be sent back to the life that has just ended. The plainness of the request is part of its pathos, since everything they had defended is now being given up in a sentence. The next verse takes up the promise they attach to it and refuses it.

phrases.translation: so I may do good in what I left behind.”
phrases.explanation: What they promise is good conduct, that they will act righteously in the life they left. The commentary explains the words as a vow to make up for the good deeds they neglected and fell short in. One early report asks pointedly what he longs to return to, whether to gather wealth or plant trees or build houses, as though to show that the resolve is not about goodness at all.

phrases.translation: Never! It is only a ˹useless˺ appeal they make.
phrases.explanation: The answer comes at once, and it is a refusal. Never, the verse says, and the commentary explains that the person will not be sent back to the world or returned to it. The words are described as a mere statement that he makes, with no power behind it. Death is not a pause that can be negotiated, and the verse closes the possibility he was hoping for.

phrases.translation: And there is a barrier behind them until the Day they are resurrected
phrases.explanation: Behind them is a barrier, and the commentary explains the word as a partition standing between them and any return, lasting until the day they are raised. It records several early descriptions of that interval, including what lies between death and resurrection. With this the passage seals its argument, that the chance to act belongs to this life, and what follows death is a waiting that no regret can cut short.

phrases.translation: Then, when the Trumpet will be blown,
phrases.explanation: The trumpet blast marks the end of the world, and the commentary records disagreement over which of the two blowings is meant here. Some held it to be the first, when everything on earth perishes. On that reading the verse describes a moment when ties of family and clan no longer join anyone, because the world in which those ties mattered has ended.

phrases.translation: there will be no kinship between them on that Day,
phrases.explanation: What is lost is kinship itself, the network of relations that had defined status and obligation in this life. The commentary explains that on that day there are no longer ties between them by which they are joined. In a society that measured a person by lineage, the statement removes the very thing people had relied on, and standing before Allah would depend on something else entirely.

phrases.translation: nor will they ˹even care to˺ ask about one another
phrases.explanation: They will not even ask about one another. The commentary explains this as their no longer visiting or enquiring about each other's circumstances and lineage, and it records a report describing each person as too absorbed in his own affair to look for anyone else. Another explanation applies the verse to the first blast, while other passages describe the people of the Garden questioning one another afterwards.

phrases.translation: As for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺,
phrases.explanation: The scale is the image of weighing, and the commentary explains a heavy scale as good deeds outweighing evil ones. Success is then defined by what follows, that such a person abides in the gardens of bliss. The verse says nothing about the size of the deeds, only about their weight, which keeps the reader from presuming to measure his own record.

phrases.translation: it is they who will be successful
phrases.explanation: Being successful repeats the word used at the very beginning of the surah for the believers. The commentary explains the success here as lasting residence in the gardens of bliss, so the opening declaration and this verse describe the same outcome. That echo is deliberate, since the qualities listed in the first verses and the weighing described here belong to one account of how a life is judged.

phrases.translation: But those whose scale is light,
phrases.explanation: The other outcome is stated with the same brevity. A light scale means good deeds are outweighed by evil, and the verse says that such people have doomed themselves. The commentary explains the loss as wronging themselves with regard to their share of Allah's mercy. The phrasing puts the responsibility on them rather than on any unfairness in the weighing.

phrases.translation: they will have doomed themselves, staying in Hell forever
phrases.explanation: The verse then names their dwelling, and the commentary explains it as remaining in the fire of Hell. The permanence is stated as plainly as the loss, and both follow from the image of the scale. The surah does not soften the contrast with the previous verse, since the two are placed side by side without comment. The reader is left with the difference between the two weights and their two ends.

phrases.translation: The Fire will burn their faces,
phrases.explanation: The fire is described as scorching their faces, and the commentary explains the word as the flame burning them. Faces are named because they are the most exposed and most recognisable part of a person, the place where dignity is read by others. The image is meant to be disturbing, and it does not soften what the previous verses have already said about their end.

phrases.translation: leaving them deformed
phrases.explanation: The result is a distortion of the face, and the commentary explains it as the lips being drawn back from the teeth because of the burning. One early report asks whether the listener has seen a head roasted in fire, with the lips pulled back and the teeth showing. The comparison is deliberately physical, and it closes the passage on the image of what the fire does.

phrases.translation: ˹It will be said,˺ “Were My revelations not recited to you,
phrases.explanation: The question put to them recalls what they were given. Were My revelations not recited to you? The commentary explains this as the verses of the Qur'an being recited to them in the world. The question is not seeking information but establishing that the warning had reached them. Being asked it in that setting makes their earlier refusal the whole point of the exchange.

phrases.translation: but you used to deny them?”
phrases.explanation: The second half names their response, that they used to deny the revelations. The commentary notes that the words introducing the speech are omitted because the context supplies them. Denial here is set against recitation, so the charge is not that they never heard but that they rejected what they heard. The next verse gives their answer, and it is not a denial of the fact.

phrases.translation: They will cry, “Our Lord! Our ill-fate took hold of us,
phrases.explanation: Their answer admits the outcome without accepting the blame. Our ill-fate took hold of us, they say, and the commentary explains this as the decree that was in Allah's foreknowledge and recorded for them overwhelming them. The wording makes their ruin sound like something done to them. Reciters differ over how the word for ill-fate is read, and both readings are treated as sound with the same meaning.

phrases.translation: so we became a misguided people
phrases.explanation: They add that they became a misguided people, which acknowledges the state but not the choice that led to it. The commentary keeps the sentence as their own confession rather than as a verdict from Allah. That is what makes the next request possible, since people who see themselves as overcome may still hope that the outcome can be reversed. The verses that follow test that hope.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Take us out of this ˹Fire˺.
phrases.explanation: The request is for another beginning. Take us out of this fire, they ask, and the commentary explains the condition they attach, that if they return to what Allah disapproves of they will be wrongdoers. The promise is complete and reasonable in form, and it is made by people who now know what they refused. The wording asks not for mercy alone but for a second chance at action.

phrases.translation: Then if we ever return ˹to denial˺, we will truly be wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: Their pledge is that they would not repeat what they had done. The commentary explains the sense as a commitment to abandon what Allah disapproved of in their deeds, with an admission that returning to it would make them wrongdoers. Everything the surah has said about their heedlessness is now reversed in a single sentence. The answer that follows shows that the time for such pledges had passed.

phrases.translation: Allah will respond, “Be despised in there!
phrases.explanation: The answer is a dismissal. Be despised in there, they are told, and the commentary explains the word as an order to remain in the fire and be driven off. Their request is refused before any reason is given. The command also marks a change in their condition, since until that point the wretched had still been hoping for deliverance.

phrases.translation: Do not ˹ever˺ plead with Me ˹again˺
phrases.explanation: The second half forbids them to speak again. Do not plead with Me, and the commentary explains that after these words they lost all hope of rescue and broke into wailing. A report describes the fire closing over them once the sentence was spoken. The verse is the point in the passage where petition ends, and everything after it explains what they had done.

phrases.translation: Indeed, there was a group of My servants who used to pray,
phrases.explanation: Allah then states the reason for the refusal. There was a group of My servants who prayed, and the prayer they used to make is quoted. The commentary explains that these were the believers who said in the world that they believed in Allah and His messengers and asked for forgiveness and mercy. Their prayer is preserved as evidence, since it shows what the mockers had been laughing at.

phrases.translation: ‘Our Lord! We have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us,
phrases.explanation: The content of the prayer is simple, belief, a request for forgiveness, and a request for mercy. The commentary explains the appeal as asking not to be punished, on the basis that Allah is the best of those who show mercy. Nothing in it claims merit or demands a reward. Its modesty stands in sharp contrast with the demands the people of the fire have just been making.

phrases.translation: for You are the best of those who show mercy,’
phrases.explanation: The final words name Allah as the best of those who show mercy, which the commentary reads as the ground of the request rather than as a conclusion to it. The believers appeal to His mercy because they have nothing else to stand on, and the surah has already described them as people who do good while afraid. Their prayer is answered, and the next verse explains at whose expense.

phrases.translation: but you were ˹so busy˺ making fun of them that it made you forget My remembrance.
phrases.explanation: The address turns to the mockers. They were so busy making fun of the believers that the mockery made them forget the remembrance of Allah. The commentary explains the forgetting as a consequence of persistent ridicule, which diverted them from remembering their Lord. The process described is gradual, and it shows how contempt for others can quietly remove a person from his own religion.

phrases.translation: And you used to laugh at them
phrases.explanation: The laughter is named as part of the charge. The commentary explains that they laughed at the believers in the world and that this conduct was what made them forget. A report compares the scene to the verse in which the criminals laugh at those who believe, until the reversal comes. The verse keeps the detail because laughter is the small, social form that hostility takes first.

phrases.translation: Today I have indeed rewarded them for their perseverance:
phrases.explanation: The reward is announced in the first person. I have rewarded them today for their perseverance, and the commentary explains that the reward is Paradise for what they patiently endured of mockery and injury. Patience here is not passive endurance but the quality that kept them faithful under ridicule. The word today marks the moment when the waiting is over and the positions are settled.

phrases.translation: they are certainly the triumphant.”
phrases.explanation: The verse ends by declaring them the triumphant. The commentary explains that the reward and the triumph are one and the same, since entering the garden is itself the victory. It also notes the reciters' disagreement over how the final clause is read, and prefers the reading that begins a fresh sentence. Either way the verse lands on the reversal.

phrases.translation: He will ask ˹them˺,
phrases.explanation: The question is put to those in the fire, and it concerns something they had once taken for granted. How many years did you remain on earth? The commentary explains that Allah asks them this while they are in the fire, and that they will answer with a figure far smaller than the truth. The question turns time itself into evidence against them.

phrases.translation: “How many years did you remain on earth?”
phrases.explanation: Years that once seemed to be the whole of a life are being counted back to them by the One who knows their number. The commentary notes that reciters differ over whether the words are read as a statement or as a command to speak, and it prefers the statement. Either way the point is the same, that the span is about to be measured from outside.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “We remained ˹only˺ a day or part of a day.
phrases.explanation: Their answer is a day or part of a day, and the commentary explains that the torment had made them forget how long they had lived, so that the years shrank in their memory to almost nothing. It notes that some of them may have lived long lives. The reply is not a lie but the effect of punishment on their sense of time.

phrases.translation: But ask those who kept count.”
phrases.explanation: Then they defer to others, saying, ask those who kept count. The commentary records disagreement over who these counters are, with some naming the angels who record deeds and others naming people who reckon months and years, and it declines to settle the question where no proof decides it. The uncertainty is left in place rather than resolved.

phrases.translation: He will say, “You only remained for a little while,
phrases.explanation: The answer comes from Allah, and it grants what they said while correcting what they thought it proved. You only remained for a little while, which the commentary explains as a brief span on earth. The sentence agrees that the time was short but denies that shortness was the point. A short life can still be decisive.

phrases.translation: if only you knew
phrases.explanation: The condition, if only you knew, turns the observation into a reproach. The commentary explains the sense as had they known the worth of their stay on earth, they would not have treated it as they did. Brevity is not an excuse but the very reason for taking the time seriously. The verse closes with a regret that arrives too late to be of use.

phrases.translation: Did you then think that We had created you without purpose,
phrases.explanation: The final question exposes the assumption behind their whole way of life. Did you think We created you without purpose? The commentary explains the words as asking whether they supposed Allah created them for sport and in vain. The question links the denial of resurrection to a view of existence without meaning, and it treats that view as the root of their conduct.

phrases.translation: and that you would never be returned to Us?”
phrases.explanation: The second half draws out the consequence, that they would never be returned to Allah. The commentary explains the error as supposing that they would not be brought back to life to be requited for what they did. Reciters differ over whether the word is read as returning or as being brought back, and both are accepted since the meaning converges. The surah ends its argument where it began, with accountability.

phrases.translation: Exalted is Allah, the True King!
phrases.explanation: The declaration returns to Allah Himself. He is exalted, the True King, and the commentary explains the exaltation as Allah being above what the polytheists ascribe to Him, whether a partner or the claim that He has daughters. The title True King sets His rule against every imagined rival, and it prepares for the denial of any other god that follows.

phrases.translation: There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him,
phrases.explanation: There is no god worthy of worship except Him, which the commentary explains as there being no object of worship deserving of worship apart from Allah, the King, the Truth. The statement is the conclusion the surah has driven toward through the answers the polytheists themselves gave. It is put as a plain fact rather than as an inference.

phrases.translation: the Lord of the Honourable Throne
phrases.explanation: The verse ends by naming Him Lord of the Honourable Throne, and the commentary explains the title as an apposition describing the same One. The throne stands for the highest created seat of authority, and its Lord is the One just declared to have no partner. The phrase closes the section on a note of majesty.

phrases.translation: Whoever invokes, besides Allah, another god—for which they can have no proof—they will surely find their penalty with their Lord.
phrases.explanation: The verse states the case of anyone who calls on another god besides Allah. The commentary explains that such a person has no argument and no proof for what he says and does. The grammar interrupts the sentence to make that point before stating the outcome, so the absence of evidence is placed at the centre of the charge rather than at its edge.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the disbelievers will never succeed
phrases.explanation: Their reckoning rests with their Lord, who will give each his due when he comes before Him. The commentary explains this as the full recompense awaiting the deed, and then states that the unbelievers will never succeed, meaning they will attain no success with Him and no lasting bliss. The verse leaves judgement where it belongs.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord! Forgive and have mercy,
phrases.explanation: The surah closes with a prayer. Forgive and have mercy, the Prophet is told to say, and the commentary explains forgiveness as the covering of sins and mercy as the acceptance of repentance and the withholding of punishment. The two requests answer the two things the surah has shown to be needed, a record that must be forgiven and a weakness that must be shown mercy.

phrases.translation: for You are the best of those who show mercy.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends with the confession that Allah is the best of those who show mercy. The commentary explains this as the mercy shown to a sinner whose repentance is accepted and who is not punished for what he did. The surah that opened with the success of the believers closes with a request for mercy, as though to say that the qualities described at the beginning are reached only through it.
